young.html: Henri Poincaré was a French mathematician who lived from 1854 to 1912. He was famous for being able to solve hard problems in his head, and for asking big questions about science itself. One of them was: which of the things scientists say are discovered, and which are choices we make?

Here is a puzzle he liked. On a flat sheet of paper, the three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. But draw a big triangle on a ball, and the angles add up to more than 180. Draw one on a saddle shape, or on a curly lettuce leaf, and they add up to less. Which world are we living in? If you only ever measure small triangles, you can’t tell!

young.name: gb-geometries
young.cap: Pick a world and grow the triangle. Small triangles add up to about 180° everywhere. Big ones show the difference.

young.html: Triangles on a ball. Take a ball or an orange. With a marker, draw a line from the top straight down to the middle (the equator), then a quarter of the way around the middle, then straight back up to the top. Look at the three corners. Each one is a square corner, 90 degrees. Three of them make 270 degrees, not 180! Now try a tiny triangle on the same ball. Does it look almost flat?

Poincaré said scientists use rules a little like the rules of a game, or like choosing to measure in inches or in centimeters. Neither one is “true”; one is just handier. But he also said real science needs experiments, because most of what science says can be checked against nature.

full.html: Henri Poincaré (1854–1912) was one of the great mathematicians of his age. He worked in nearly every part of mathematics and physics: the motion of planets (his prize-winning study of the three-body problem in 1889 opened the way to what we now call chaos theory), the shape of spaces (topology), light and electricity, and the new physics of moving electrons, where in 1905 he reached some of the same results as Einstein’s relativity. He also wrote clear books for general readers about what science is.

La Science et l’hypothèse appeared in Paris in 1902. W. J. Greenstreet’s English translation came out in 1905, with an introduction by the physicist Joseph Larmor. Two more books followed, The Value of Science (1905) and Science and Method (1908).

Some people think science gives us certain truth. Others think it is all guesswork. Poincaré rejects both. In his preface he says that the skeptic has the lazy answer, and that we should look carefully at what role each kind of hypothesis plays.

full.text: This sceptical attitude does not escape the charge of superficiality. To doubt everything or to believe everything are two equally convenient solutions; both dispense with the necessity of reflection.
full.author: Henri Poincaré

full.html: The book moves through four parts: number and magnitude, space, force and nature. In each, Poincaré sorts the statements of science into kinds.

head: Part
What Poincaré argues
rows: Proof by mathematical induction (if a rule holds for 1, and holding for n makes it hold for n + 1, it holds for every whole number) is the true engine of mathematics. It is not mere logic, and not learned from experience: it rests on the mind’s power to imagine a step repeated without end.
The axioms of geometry are neither forced on us by reason nor discovered by measuring. They are conventions: free choices, guided by experience, which we keep because they are convenient.
Several principles of mechanics, such as the law of inertia, began in experiment but have been raised to the rank of definitions that no single experiment can overturn.
Physics also needs real hypotheses, which experiment can confirm or refute. A good theory may be replaced and still leave behind true relations between things.

full.html: In the 1800s Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann had built geometries in which Euclid’s parallel postulate fails. In one, the angles of a triangle add to less than 180°; in another, to more. Each is as consistent as Euclid’s. So which is the geometry of real space?

Poincaré imagined beings living in a great sphere where it grows colder toward the edge, and every ruler shrinks as it moves outward. Such beings, measuring carefully, would find that the geometry of their world is not Euclid’s. Yet we could just as well describe their world with Euclid’s geometry plus a law about temperature. Measurement always involves both geometry and physics, so experiment alone can’t pick the geometry.

full.text: What, then, are we to think of the question: Is Euclidean geometry true? It has no meaning. We might as well ask if the metric system is true, and if the old weights and measures are false; if Cartesian co-ordinates are true and polar co-ordinates false. One geometry cannot be more true than another; it can only be more convenient.
full.author: Henri Poincaré
full.work: Science and Hypothesis, Chapter III, Non-Euclidean Geometries

full.name: gb-geometries
full.cap: The same equilateral triangle in a flat, a spherical and a saddle-shaped world. On a sphere the extra angle (the spherical excess) grows with the area.

full.title: The angles of a big triangle
full.q: On a sphere, a triangle’s angles add to 180° plus an extra amount called the spherical excess E, and its area is (E ÷ 180°) × π R². A triangle on the Earth (R ≈ 6,371 km) runs from the North Pole down to the equator, a quarter of the way around, and back up. Find its angles, its excess and its area.
steps: Each corner is a right angle: 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°.
Check: that is one eighth of the whole surface, 4π R² ≈ 510 million km².
full.a: Three 90° angles; excess 90°; about 64 million km², one eighth of the globe.

full.title: Reasoning by recurrence
full.q: Show that 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n² for every n.
steps: Suppose it holds for n. The next odd number is 2n + 1, so the new sum is n² + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)².
So if it holds for n, it holds for n + 1. Starting from 1, it holds for 2, then 3, and so on forever.
full.a: True for every n. This kind of step, Poincaré said, is where mathematics leaves pure logic behind and makes something new.

full.html: Poincaré’s conventionalism: some basic statements of science, especially the axioms of geometry and certain principles of mechanics, are neither self-evident truths nor experimental facts but agreed definitions, chosen because they are simple and useful. Most other scientific statements remain open to testing.

Thinking Poincaré meant that science is just made up. He said the opposite: conventions are few, and they are guided by experience; the rest of science is answerable to experiment, and its lasting gains are real relations between things.

The book was widely read. In Bern, around 1902–1904, the young Albert Einstein and his friends in their small reading circle, the “Olympia Academy,” studied it closely. But Einstein’s general relativity (1915) described gravity as the curving of space and time, and astronomers came to treat the geometry of space as something measured, not chosen. Poincaré had expected Euclid to remain the most convenient choice. Philosophers still debate how much of his conventionalism survives; many agree he was right that a theory meets experiment as a whole, geometry and physics together.

items: Euclid, earlier on this ladder, built geometry on a few postulates. The fifth, about parallels, troubled readers for two thousand years. Poincaré explains why other choices are possible.
Kant held that Euclid’s geometry is known a priori, before any experience. Poincaré agreed that the mind brings something of its own (in mathematical induction) but denied that it imposes Euclid.
Einstein’s Relativity, the next rungs on, makes geometry part of physics.
Whitehead and Russell tried to build mathematics from logic. Poincaré was a sharp critic of that program.
Which parts of what you were taught in science are facts you could check, and which are choices of words or units?
If two descriptions of the world fit every possible measurement equally well, is there any sense in which one is true?
Can an experiment ever test one statement on its own, or only a whole web of them?

questions: Inches or centimeters: is one of them more true? What makes one more convenient for a job?
Why can’t a person measuring small triangles in a garden tell whether the Earth is round?
Poincaré says doubting everything is as lazy as believing everything. Do you agree? Why?
Think of a rule in a game you play. Could the game work with a different rule? Would it be a worse game, or just a different one?
Einstein read this book as a young man. What questions in it might have set him thinking?
